paper_title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

sections.content: RoboEvo2: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via HarnessPolicy Co-Evolution Jiehong Lin1,, Wei Huang1 Xuzhao Huang1 Chenzhi Liu1, Haoyuan Li2 Yang Zhang3 Junchao Huang4 Chenyeyang Cai2 Bo Wang1 Kazuhiro Kosuge5 Zhongrui Wang3 Xiaojuan Qi1, 1The University of Hong Kong 2Zhejiang University 3Southern University of Science and Technology 4The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 5City University of Hong Kong Equal contribution Project leader Corresponding author: xjqi@eee.hku.hk Project page: kaiknower.github.io/RoboEvo2 Code: github.com/kaiknower/RoboEvo2 Figure 1. Overview of RoboEvo2. Co-evolution loop (top): the policy is rolled out on task batch, and failed tasks are passed to coding agent, which repairs the harness through parallel Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes. Verified repairs are kept as skills, memory, and routing rules, and the verified trajectories update the policy. Results (bottom): on LIBERO-PRO and RoboTwin C2R, success of the policy alone and with the harness rises while API cost falls over rounds; in MolmoSpaces, the system improves on tasks it proposes itself; on the Unitree G1-D, the harness evolved in RoboTwin transfers to the real robot and collects the demonstrations that train the policy.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo2, framework for recursive harnesspolicy co-evolution. In Policyto-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo2 improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demon1 strate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1D. Our models and code will be publicly released. 1. Introduction Robots should adapt rapidly to unfamiliar environments, acquire new skills through interaction, and execute those skills efficiently with practice. Human learning motivates this progression from deliberate problem solving to fluent execution, while retaining the flexibility to tackle new situations. Current robot systems offer complementary strengths toward this goal. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) [2, 3, 15, 45] and world action models (WAMs) [11, 13, 41] enable efficient visuomotor control, but remain vulnerable to task and scene shifts [30, 46]. Adapting them through imitation learning often requires collecting many additional human demonstrations, making continual skill acquisition costly. Foundation-model agents can draw on broad prior knowledge, reason about unfamiliar situations, and invoke robot-control APIs to discover and refine solutions [10, 21, 43, 44]. However, repeated reasoning, tool use, and repair introduce latency and API costs that limit reliance on agentic execution for routine behavior. Realizing this progression requires reciprocal learning loop between an agents harnessits executable skills, memory, and orchestrationand its low-level policy. Harness-centered recursive self-improvement methods refine programs and accumulate experience through feedback [9, 20, 32, 35], but keeping the motor policy fixed does not transfer newly acquired skills into the learned controller. Policy-centered methods use foundation models to guide autonomous data collection and improve learned controllers [12, 23, 47], but do not jointly adapt the harness to the controllers changing abilities. Co-evolution must therefore connect learning efficient policy behaviors from harness discoveries with adapting the harness to the improving policy. This reciprocity is essential because policy improvement changes both the motor skills available to the agent and the failures that still require exploration and repair. We introduce RoboEvo2, framework for recursive harnesspolicy co-evolution that uses current-policy failures to drive both updates  (Fig. 1)  . In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, coding agent diagnoses failures, discovers verified corrections, and consolidates them into reusable skills, routing strategies, and persistent memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, successful trajectories and matched failurecorrection pairs teach the policy to reproduce effective corrections and disfavor failed alternatives. The updated policy then supplies stronger motor skills for subsequent agentic search, while its remaining failures redirect harness refinement. Concurrent studies also investigate harnesspolicy coupling [4, 7, 34, 36]. RoboEvo2 connects failure-guided, multi-route solution discovery with explicit learning from matched failures and corrections, progressively reducing repeated agentic intervention as acquired skills are internalized into the policy. First, to discover complementary capabilities, we develop failure-conditioned, multi-route P2H repair engine. For each policy failure, it searches three solution routes in parallel: Code refines control programs, Code+ICL incorporates demonstration guidance, and Code+Policy composes programs with learned motor skills. Execution feedback drives iterative repair, and the successful candidate with the lowest normalized motion jerk is selected under matched conditions. This design combines complementary control capabilities to generate verified, smooth corrections targeted at current policy weaknesses. Second, to internalize corrective capabilities, we introduce Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD). CPD pairs failed and corrected continuations from the same starting state and optimizes margin between their actionprediction losses relative to frozen reference policy. Asymmetric proximity penalties discourage degradation of corrective behaviors and excessive suppression of failed alternatives. Combined with supervised learning on verified trajectories, CPD teaches both which corrections to reproduce and which failed alternatives to disfavor. Failureaware sampling and continual-learning regularization support targeted acquisition and capability retention. Third, to sustain iterative capability reuse, we develop harness update mechanism coupled with policy reuse across rounds. Compatible repairs update executable skills and routing logic, while persistent memory retains failure contexts, attempted solutions, and validated guidance. The updated policy then drives subsequent rollouts and participates in Code+Policy search, changing both the failures requiring exploration and the motor primitives available for repair. This closes the reciprocal loop: accumulated harness knowledge supports correction discovery, while internalized policy capabilities directly support subsequent search. Experiments demonstrate recursive adaptation to distribution shifts without additional human demonstrations. Across eight rounds on LIBERO-PRO [46] and five rounds on RoboTwin C2R [5], standalone success improves from 11.0% to 84.1% and 46.0% to 77.5%, respectively, with hybrid success reaching 90.5% and 87.4% alongside reduced agentic API expenditure. On RoboTwin C2R, our method with 7.5K trajectories matches conventional training with 27.5K trajectories. Ablations validate reciprocal co-evolution, complementary solution routes in P2H, and counterfactual preference distillation in H2P. We further demonstrate autonomous task acquisition on MolmoSpaces [16] and cross-embodiment harness transfer. On the Unitree G1-D, simulation-evolved harness enables the collection of 120 demonstrations, yielding 85.0% 2 standalone success compared with 80.0% using 200 human demonstrations, while fixed-harness hybrid execution reaches 95.0%. 2. Related Work Continual Robot Learning. continually learning policy must retain earlier skills and obtain supervision for new ones. For retention, EWC regularizes weights [17], ER replays data [29], and PackNet isolates parameters [27]. In manipulation, LOTUS builds skill libraries [33] and TAIL uses task-specific adapters [25]. On pretrained VLAs, experience replay mitigates forgetting [24, 48]; PHASER refines it by prioritizing phases most at risk of forgetting [6], while CRL-VLA limits advantage magnitudes on prior tasks during continual RL [42]. For new supervision, HG-DAgger and RECAP draw on human interventions during policy rollouts [1, 14], APO and FlowPRO turn such interventions into preference signals [38, 39], and SOAR uses autonomous VLM-guided practice [47]. RoboEvo2 learns from verified harness repairs of policy failures rather than operator corrections, and employs failure-aware task sampling to retain skills and improve low-success tasks. Agentic Self-Improvement. Agentic systems such as Code as Policies [21], Harness VLA [44], RATs [43], and ASPIRE [26] solve tasks through programs, skills, and memory without model fine-tuning. Among recursive selfimprovement (RSI) frameworks, Zetta, EmbodiedEvo, EmbodiedRSI, and RPG evolve only the harness [9, 20, 32, 35], whereas ENPIRE and EmbodiRSI focus on policy improvement [18, 40]. Co-Harness and Self-HPO alternate harness and model updates for LLM agents [7, 37]. AdaRSI [34] refines its harness and fine-tunes only sub-steps that still fail when retried from saved states. However, these methods train the policy only to imitate successful executions. In contrast, RoboEvo2 also learns from failures: it pairs failed continuation with verified repair from the same state and trains the policy to prefer the repair. Repairs are sought in parallel along code-only, demonstration-guided, and policy-calling routes. 3. RoboEvo2 3.1. Overview of Recursive Co-Evolution RoboEvo2 is policy-driven framework for recursive harnesspolicy co-evolution. The current policy exposes capability gaps through execution failures, the harness discovers effective solutions, and the policy subsequently internalizes these corrections. As illustrated in Fig. 2, RoboEvo2 jointly evolves an agentic harness Hr = (Lr, Mr, ρr) and neural policy πθr at evolution round r. The harness consists of an executable skill library Lr, persistent experience memory Mr, and routing mechanism ρr for skill invocation and codepolicy coordination. We initialize H0 with robot APIs and parameterized codebased skills from CaP-X [10] and RATs [43]. The initial policy πθ0 is obtained by fine-tuning pretrained VLA or WAM on robot demonstrations D0. Each evolution round consists of four stages: (1) Policy Rollouts. The current policy πθr serves as the primary executor, generating task rollouts Tr. Task-level verification partitions them into successful trajectories Sr and failed trajectories Fr. The failures identify where additional capabilities are needed. (2) Policy-to-Harness Evolution (P2H). For each failed rollout, VLM-based coding agent (GPT-6 Astra) diagnoses the failure and searches for solutions through three complementary routes: Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy. Verified solutions are selected based on execution quality, and compatible improvements are integrated across failures into candidate harness (cid:101)Hr+1. Execution and repair experiences are retained for subsequent reuse (Sec. 3.2). (3) Harness-to-Policy Evolution (H2P). Successful policy rollouts and harness-generated corrections are accumulated as training data. Matched successful and failed executions further provide counterfactual supervision. Task-balanced, failure-aware sampling and policy optimization produce an updated candidate policy π (cid:101)θr+1 (4) Evaluation and Selection. We evaluate two execution modes: standalone, where the policy executes tasks independently, and hybrid, where the harness coordinates policy execution with reusable code skills. Candidate and previous versions are compared on matched development tasks, initial states, and execution budgets. Updates are retained when they improve the corresponding success rates; otherwise, previous versions are preserved. The selected pair (Hr+1, πθr+1) enters the next round. Further details are provided in Appendix D. (Sec. 3.3). By repeatedly discovering and internalizing missing capabilities, RoboEvo2 forms recursive improvement loop driven by the evolving policys remaining failures. 3.2. Policy-to-Harness (P2H) Evolution P2H evolution discovers executable solutions to capability gaps exposed by the current policy. Rather than relying on the coding agent to solve tasks independently from scratch, P2H targets failed policy executions and converts successful corrections into reusable harness capabilities. Given Fr, it first searches for solutions to individual failures and then consolidates the verified results across tasks. Failure-Guided Solution Search and Selection. For each failed rollout Fr, VLM-based coding agent diagnoses the failure using policy observations, action history, and task outcomes. It retrieves relevant skills from Lr and past experiences from Mr, then explores three complementary solution routes in parallel: 3 Figure 2. P2H and H2P evolution. (a) P2H: for each failure in Fr, the VLM coding agent retrieves memory, diagnoses the failure, and searches Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes in parallel; it keeps the verified solution with the lowest jerk J(τ ) and merges compatible changes into the skills L, memory , and routing ρ of (cid:101)Hr+1. (b) H2P: verified trajectories and same-state success/failure pairs update the policy with SFT, CPD, and EWC under failure-aware task sampling; the updated policy starts round r+1. Code: The agent first attempts recovery using the codebased skills in the current harness. If unsuccessful, it refines executable skills, including motion targets, grasp and contact strategies, phase transitions, and recovery logic based on execution feedback. Code+ICL: The agent randomly samples one demonstration for the target task from D0 to guide harness refinement. It extracts task structure, manipulation strategies, and temporal cues to revise executable skills, including object-relative motions, arm coordination, gripper control, and execution sequencing. The revisions are then tested and iteratively improved via execution feedback. Code+Policy: The agent first attempts recovery by coordinating code-based skills in the current harness with the policy πθr as learned motor primitive. If unsuccessful, it refines harness orchestration, including subgoal allocation, skill composition, policy invocation, handoff conditions, and recovery strategies. This route exploits the complementary capabilities of code and learned policies. The three routes explore different solution strategies while sharing the same task goal and execution constraints. Each route operates in an isolated execution branch, starting from the relevant failure state when feasible or from matched task reset otherwise. Execution and refinement continue until task success or budget exhaustion, while the policy parameters remain frozen throughout P2H. Each route retains at most one verified successful programtrajectory pair for failure , forming candidate set C+ of up to three solutions. Among successful candidates evaluated under matched conditions, we select the one with the lowest normalized motion jerk J(τ ) [19]: = (c , τ ) arg min (c,τ )C+ J(τ ), (1) and τ where denote the selected executable program and verified trajectory, respectively. If no candidate succeeds, the failure remains unresolved and is retained for diagnosis. Importantly, each resolved failure associates the original failed policy execution with verified successful correction. These execution records provide targeted supervision for subsequent policy learning, including matched corrective pairs for CPD when the corresponding state and execution conditions are satisfied (Sec. 3.3). Further implementation details are provided in Appendices and C. Cross-Failure Harness Integration. Beyond individual recovery, P2H consolidates successful solutions into persistent capabilities that can be reused across tasks. The coding agent merges compatible modifications from selected solutions into unified candidate harness (cid:101)Hr+1. The skill library Lr is extended with new or refined executable programs, while the routing mechanism ρr is updated when skill selection, subgoal coordination, or code policy switching changes. Meanwhile, memory Mr accumulates failure contexts, attempted solutions, execution outcomes, and validated repair guidance. Successful recovery does not necessarily require modifying code; solutions using existing skills still contribute verified trajectories and reusable experience. The integrated harness is checked for compatibility and evaluated before replacing Hr, preventing individual repairs from automatically becoming persistent system updates. Further details are provided in Appendix A. 3.3. Harness-to-Policy (H2P) Evolution H2P evolution aims to internalize agent-discovered corrective behaviors into the neural policy. It leverages two complementary forms of supervision. First, successful policy rollouts Sr and verified harness-generated trajectories H,+ , including full-task solutions and recovery continur ations, are accumulated in Dr+1 for supervised learning. Second, matched policy failures and successful corrections form corrective preference dataset Pr+1 for Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD), which encourages the policy to favor corrected behaviors over failed alternatives. Counterfactual Preference Distillation. We build Pr+1 by pairing original policy failures with verified harnessgenerated corrections. For each resolved failure, successful and failed continuations are compared from the same starting state under matched execution conditions. After offline co-evolution, compatible action policies can be further refined using PPO [31], which collects fresh simulator rollouts and optimizes task-success rewards. 3.4. Standalone and Hybrid Execution Modes RoboEvo2 supports two complementary execution modes that balance policy autonomy and agentic assistance: Standalone Execution: The co-evolved policy executes tasks directly without coding-agent intervention, enabling efficient neural inference while leveraging capabilities acquired from agentic corrections. Hybrid Execution: An embodied agent coordinates the co-evolved policy with reusable code skills, supporting explicit task decomposition, skill composition, and feedback-driven recovery [44]. Through recursive co-evolution, policy failures drive the discovery of new executable capabilities, while agentic corrections are progressively internalized into the policy. As the policy improves, its evolving capability gaps guide subsequent harness evolution, forming self-reinforcing cycle of discovery and learning. This process aims to amortize costly agentic reasoning into efficient policy execution, progressively reducing reliance on agentic assistance while retaining the harness for unresolved challenges. 4. Experiments We evaluate RoboEvo2 on LIBERO-PRO [46] and RoboTwin C2R [5] for multi-round co-evolution and generalization to unseen perturbations, with ablations examining reciprocal evolution, P2H solution routes, and CPD. MolmoSpaces [16] evaluates autonomous capability acquisition, while cross-embodiment and Unitree G1-D experiments demonstrate harness reusability, sim-to-real transfer, and real-world policy learning. 4.1. Generalization and Multi-Round Evolution We evaluate RoboEvo2 on two benchmarks under distribution shifts. LIBERO-PRO [46] transfers policies trained on original LIBERO demonstrations to task and position perturbations, while RoboTwin C2R [5] adapts policies trained on 2,500 clean demonstrations to randomized scenes across 50 bimanual tasks. On both benchmarks, evolution runs on seeds held out from the initial training data without additional human annotation, and generalization is evaluated on separate unseen seeds (800 LIBERO-PRO and 5,000 RoboTwin C2R episodes; Appendix D). Multi-Round Adaptation and Data Efficiency. Figure 3 demonstrates progressive improvements in standalone and hybrid execution. On LIBERO-PRO, eight rounds improve standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5%, while API expenditure decreases from $430.63 to $98.92. On RoboTwin C2R, five rounds increase standalone success from 46.0% to 77.5% and hybrid success from 48.8% to 87.4%, with API expenditure decreasing from $719.05 to $323.84. These results demonstrate sustained capability improvement alongside decreasing agentic costs, highlighting the benefits of recursive harnesspolicy co-evolution. Beyond execution efficiency, RoboEvo2 acquires training experience without additional human demonstrations. As shown in Tab. 1, starting from 2,500 clean demonstrations, our framework autonomously collects 5,000 verified trajectories and achieves 77.5% standalone success on RoboTwin C2R. With the same 7.5K trajectories, clean+random training reaches only 67.2%, and it needs 27.5K to reach 76.8%. RoboEvo2 thus matches it with only 27.3% of the training data, suggesting that failure-driven experience provides effective supervision. Comparison with Self-Evolving Methods. Table 2 compares RoboEvo2 with recent self-evolving robot systems. Harness-centered methods, including ASPIRE [26], Zetta [9], DynaHarness [8], and EmbodiedRSI [32], primarily improve executable skills and agentic recovery. In contrast, RoboEvo2 enables reciprocal evolution, where harness discoveries provide corrective supervision for policy learning, while the updated policy supplies stronger motor primitives and guides subsequent harness search. Across all eight LIBERO-PRO settings, RoboEvo2 achieves 84.1% standalone and 90.5% hybrid success, surpassing EmbodiedRSIs 86.8% hybrid success. Further PPO refinement increases standalone and hybrid success to 94.8% and 96.8%, respectively. Unlike code-only agents such as CaP-Agent0 [10] and RATs [43], we extend the exploration process of RATs by incorporating trainable policy within our harnesspolicy co-evolution framework. Verified agentic executions are used to improve the policy, enabling acquired skills to be internalized beyond executable programs. As shown in Tab. 7, the frozen harness achieves 45.8% success on ALOHA AgileX, 42.5% on dual ARX-X5, and 41.0% on dual Franka-Panda. The small performance drops indicate that evolved harness capabilities can transfer across robot embodiments without additional skill evolution. 4.4. Real-World Robot Manipulation We evaluate RoboEvo2 on four bimanual tasks  (Fig. 4)  using the Unitree G1-D, investigating whether simulationevolved harness capabilities can transfer to physical robots and provide training supervision without teleoperation. Harness Transfer and Autonomous Data Collection. We directly transfer the harness evolved on RoboTwin to the Unitree G1-D, adapting only the robot interfaces and estimating motion targets from real observations. Using its frozen Code route, the transferred harness collects 10 verified demonstrations per task. We first fine-tune π0.5 on these trajectories and execute the resulting policy on the physical robot. When execution fails, an operator approximately restores the robot and scene to the pre-failure state, without teleoperating the corrective actions. The agent then explores Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, selecting verified corrections with the lowest normalized motion jerk. This process collects 20 additional successful trajectories per task, yielding 120 automatically generated demonstrations in total. We use these trajectories and eligible corrective pairs to train the final standalone policy through H2P. Real-World Results. As shown in Tab. 8, the transferred Figure 4. Real-world executions on the Unitree G1-D. harness achieves 47.5% mean success without target-side skill evolution. The RoboEvo2 policy trained on 120 automatically collected demonstrations achieves 85.0% standalone success, compared with 80.0% for π0.5 baseline trained on 200 human-teleoperated demonstrations. Combining the learned policy with the fixed harness further increases success to 95.0%. These results demonstrate that reusable harness capabilities can support sim-to-real execution and generate effective policy supervision with limited human intervention, while hybrid execution continues to complement the learned policy. 5. Conclusion We presented RoboEvo2, framework for failure-driven recursive harnesspolicy co-evolution. Through complementary solution discovery (P2H) and counterfactual capability internalization (H2P), verified agentic corrections become reusable harness skills and learned policy behaviors. Across rounds, the improved policy provides stronger motor primitives and redirects subsequent harness exploration, closing the reciprocal learning loop. Experiments demonstrate progressive improvements in standalone and hybrid execution with reduced agentic costs, alongside data-efficient adaptation, autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment reuse, and real-world policy learning. RoboEvo2 thus supports progressive policy autonomy while retaining agentic capabilities for unresolved challenges.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: An LLM-based assistant (OpenAI Codex) was used for language editing, LaTeX formatting, and checking bibliographic metadata. All assisted content was reviewed and verified by the authors. Separately, as part of the method, RoboEvo2 uses GPT-6 Astra as its coding agent (Qwen3.827B in the agent-backbone ablation; see Appendix G). No LLM is listed as an author; the authors take full responsibility for the manuscript, implementation, experiments, and scientific claims.

The Coding Astra run with reasoning effort xhigh; (gpt-6-astra), it is used both for coding and for demonstration video analysis. Each coding call receives the task instruction, recorded camera frames, the localized failure, retrieved memory entries, and the editable skill programs, and returns program revision; the prompts are given in Appendix E. After each round we save the accepted code, memory, policy checkpoint, and data manifest. Skill library. The skill library Lr holds only executable code, separate from memory Mr and routing ρr. It is organized as two-level skill tree. At the bottom are atomic skills: observing, gripper commands, relative motions, motions to target anchored at an image pixel, and policy calls, which only Code+Policy may use. Above them are composite skills, each composed from atomic skills and parameterized by its arguments, such as grasping, placing, transferring, pulling, and stroking along surface. program calls skills by name with arguments. Extending Lr adds new entry, and refining skill writes new revision of its entry while earlier revisions are kept. Figure 6 shows how general skills are specialized and how memory grows on LIBEROPRO. Memory. Memory Mr has two parts. General memory holds lessons that apply across tasks, grouped by skill category (perception, grasping, placing, contact, policy, and motion and planning). Experiences are learned from individual tasks: each entry states when it applies, the action to take, and the skills it uses, and is retrieved by matching the task instruction. An experience that holds across tasks is promoted to general memory  (Fig. 6)  . Routing. Routing ρr is set of rules in the agents instructions rather than separate model. In hybrid execution, code staging precedes each policy call, and after the call the agent re-observes before choosing the next step. Updating ρr edits these rules. Figure 5 shows the routing on one recorded LIBERO-PRO episode. A.2. Solution Routes Route capabilities. Each route evolves its own skill library and memory from the same initial harness; the routes use the same coding model, observations, verifier, and budgets and differ only in what else the agent may use. Code calls code skills only and receives no demonstration. Code+ICL additionally receives demonstration of the task in context and cannot call the policy. Code+Policy can additionally call the current policy with short local instruction, Figure 5. Hybrid deployment. The agent with memory Mr routes each step of recorded LIBERO-PRO episode to the policy πθ or code skill (routing ρ). and receives no demonstration. In every route, the agents program is executed from the failure state or from the original reset; the failure state is restored by replaying the policys recorded actions. Each repair work item contains the parent harness revision, the task and its initial state, the original goal and verifier, the localized failure, the affected skill, retrieved repair cases, and trial budget.
